content.p: On the evening of 20 October 2020, gunfire broke out over a crowd of young people who had camped for days at the Lekki toll gate in Lagos, singing the national anthem and waving the Nigerian flag. They were part of #EndSARS, a nationwide protest movement against police brutality. CNN wrote that the shooting quashed the movement, and for more than a year the federal government denied that protesters had been shot at the toll gate, while the army denied that its soldiers had shot at them.

In November 2021 a panel set up by the Lagos state government reported that soldiers had fired on unarmed protesters without provocation, that police had also shot at them, and that the killings could, in context, be described as a massacre. Nigeria's federal information minister called the leaked report the triumph of fake news. CNN reported in October 2021 that no one had taken responsibility or been held to account, and none of the later pages consulted, which run to November 2021, reports a prosecution.
content.h2: From a viral video to a curfew
content.p: The protests began after a video shared on 3 October 2020 appeared to show officers of the Special Anti-Robbery Squad, known as SARS, dragging two men from a hotel and shooting one of them, according to Amnesty International. Global Citizen describes the unit as created in 1992 to fight robbery and later criticised as corrupt and responsible for extrajudicial killings. Nationwide demonstrations began on 8 October. Amnesty says SARS was disbanded on 11 October, under President Muhammadu Buhari's government. Amnesty noted that this was the fifth time since 2015 that the authorities had pledged to reform or disband the unit, and the protests continued with wider demands for police reform and better governance.

The Lekki toll gate, on a major road in an affluent part of Lagos, became the movement's most visible site. According to CNN, protesters across the country put up tents and DJ booths and held multi-faith prayers, and a "festival of lights" for victims of police brutality was held at the toll gate. Al Jazeera reported that the Lagos government imposed a round-the-clock curfew, and that the crowd stayed despite it. The BBC put the number at the toll gate that day at some 1,000.

Amnesty International, in a timeline it published on 28 October, said it had tracked army vehicles from Bonny Camp, a barracks Al Jazeera put about 5 kilometres from the toll gate, using photographs and videos posted on social media. It said two military vehicles were filmed leaving at 6:29 p.m. and that more vehicles that appeared to belong to the military and police were filmed afterwards. CNN, which analysed protesters' video, put the moment its video shows the army appearing to fire directly at protesters at 6:47 p.m. Witnesses described to Al Jazeera men in army fatigues arriving at about 7 p.m. and raising their guns after the demonstrators had knelt to wave flags and sing the anthem. The BBC reported that soldiers were reportedly seen barricading the site moments before the shooting started, and that shots could be heard on video as protesters sat with locked arms.

Before the shooting, according to Amnesty, it had received reports that the CCTV cameras at the toll gates had been removed by government officials and that the electricity had been cut. Al Jazeera, reporting the panel's findings, wrote that men believed to be state government officials had tampered with surveillance equipment earlier that day, but that events were captured by social media live streams. A soldier who spoke to Reuters without being named told the agency that troops from the army's 81st Division, 65th Battalion, based at Bonny Camp, had fired on unarmed civilians.

The aftermath was filmed too. The BBC noted that live footage showed protesters tending to the wounded. Amnesty said credible evidence showed the military prevented ambulances from reaching the severely injured, and eyewitnesses told CNN the army removed a number of bodies. Amnesty also alleged that the military took away some casualties from the toll plaza and from Alausa, another Lagos neighbourhood.

The sources give different tolls, and CNN wrote in October 2021 that there was no official death toll. On 21 October 2020 Amnesty International said security forces had fired on two gatherings in Lagos, at Lekki and Alausa, killing at least 12 people. It also said 38 people had died across Nigeria on that Tuesday and at least 56 since the protests began, a total that it said included protesters and "thugs who were allegedly hired by the authorities". It has since repeated the figure of at least 12 for the two sites.

Lagos governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu put the injured at 25 and said the single death was from blunt trauma to the head. The BBC later reported the state government's figures as 30 injured and one death, and Al Jazeera wrote that he had said there were only two fatalities. The army's representative, Brigadier Ahmed Taiwo, told the panel that one death, by blunt force to the head, happened on Admiralty Way, about 3 kilometres from the toll gate, and another at Yaba, and that neither had anything to do with the toll gate.

The judicial panel's own tally was 48 casualties. HumAngle reported them as 11 dead, 24 missing and 8 assaulted by soldiers and police. Al Jazeera, describing the same report, wrote that there were 11 killed and four missing. Vanguard said at least 48 protesters were shot dead, wounded or assaulted, and that the real number could be higher because many victims feared giving evidence. A forensic pathologist, Professor John Obafunwa, told the panel that three bodies from the toll gate had been deposited at Mainland Hospital in Yaba, and that the autopsies showed death from bleeding caused by penetrating objects or a rifled weapon. The panel reasoned that the unidentified bodies on a list of 96 others could include victims from Lekki. CNN, a year on, wrote that there was still no official death toll.

One account in CNN's anniversary report is from a mother CNN calls Adesola, a name that is not her real one. She said she reached the toll gate at around 5 or 6 a.m. and found her 32-year-old son with a bullet wound to the chest, still breathing. He died in her arms in a car, she said, and was buried almost at once under Muslim rites. Others, CNN wrote, had not found the bodies of missing relatives.

The army's account changed repeatedly. In the first days it denied involvement and described reports as fake news. Late on the Tuesday after the shooting a spokesman, Major Osoba Olaniyi, acknowledged that soldiers had been sent to enforce the curfew, on orders from the Lagos state government, while insisting that "at no time did soldiers of the Nigerian army open fire on any civilian". Sanwo-Olu replied that no governor controls the army's rules of engagement, and said he had ordered an investigation into them. The army then said its soldiers fired in the air and used blanks, and that hoodlums were mixed into the crowd, CNN reported.

On 14 November, giving evidence to the panel, Brigadier Taiwo told it that the soldiers had carried live rounds for protection, but that the firing team, who could be seen in the video, had magazines charged with blanks. He told the panel that his troops' "only crime was to report for duty to protect us all". According to the BBC, he also said a casualty one witness had seen had been overcome by shock.

The federal government's line was harder. Information Minister Lai Mohammed called the incident a "phantom massacre", and CNN reported that on the first anniversary he again dismissed its investigation as fake news. After CNN published that investigation on 19 November 2020, the Ministry of Information wrote to the network on 23 November asking for an internal inquiry. The letter said the government reserved the right to act within its laws. CNN stood by its reporting. The police said in a tweet in early November that their officers never used unlawful force or shot protesters, as CNN reported.

The Judicial Panel of Inquiry and Restitution had been commissioned by the Lagos government to examine allegations of police abuse, including by SARS. According to Al Jazeera, the governor then expanded its terms of reference to take in the Lekki shooting. Al Jazeera's report of 28 October 2020 said it had begun investigating the shooting on the Tuesday of that week, and it delivered a 309-page report on 15 November 2021.

The panel found that army officers shot, injured and killed unarmed protesters without provocation or justification while they waved the flag and sang the anthem. It found that police deployed to the toll gate that night shot at, assaulted and battered unarmed protesters, leading to injuries and deaths, and tried to cover up by picking up bullets. It found the army had refused to let ambulances give help to the wounded and had not followed its own rules of engagement. It concluded that soldiers shot blank and live rounds into the crowd "with the deliberate intention to assault, maim and kill".

The panel said it preferred the testimony of petitioners and witnesses to that of General Taiwo, who had not been at the toll gate. It cited a ballistics expert who said that video showed troops re-arming their weapons before firing into the air or purposely in the direction of the protesters. The panel also said that two spent shells recovered when it visited the site on 30 October 2020 were consistent with ammunition normally used by the army and had been fired live, according to its forensic analyst.

It also made findings about the clean-up. It said three trucks of the Lagos State Waste Management Authority with brushes underneath arrived on the morning of 21 October to clean away bloodstains and other evidence. It said the company that operates the toll gate, the Lekki Concession Company, refused to hand over some information and tendered incomplete CCTV footage that had been manipulated. The company had told the panel on 3 November that the recording stopped at about 8 p.m. because it had been tampered with. CNN's own comparison of the footage found that at 6:47 p.m. the camera panned away from the area where CNN had video of soldiers appearing to fire at protesters, and it said it could not tell whether that was deliberate.

Its recommendations were severe. According to CNN, the panel urged that all army personnel who were deployed to the toll gate, except one major general, face disciplinary action, be stripped of status and be dismissed, calling them unfit to serve in any public or security service. It recommended that the army be discouraged from internal security duties and that a monument bearing the victims' names be built at the toll gate. It also recommended that remaining petitions it could not resolve in time go to a human rights tribunal. Separately, Justice Okuwobi was quoted in a Lagos government statement saying that about 70 victims of police brutality had been awarded 410 million naira, around one million dollars.

The inquiry had its own troubles. Al Jazeera reported that Rinu Oduala, a youth representative on the panel, resigned saying she would not "be part of a cover-up". It added that Lieutenant Colonel Sanusi Ovada Bello, believed to have led the troops from Bonny Camp, received two summonses and did not appear, and that other army officials repeatedly ignored summonses for months.

Sanwo-Olu said the state would issue a white paper and appointed a four-person committee, led by the state attorney general, to review the report. The federal response was different. On 23 November 2021 Lai Mohammed said the report was "nothing but the triumph of fake news and the intimidation of a silent majority by a vociferous lynch mob", and that its authenticity was in doubt because it had leaked. Segun Awosanya, a panel member, told CNN that the panel had worked objectively, that hard copies had been delivered to the Lagos government and that a leak should not be the government's problem.

Amnesty International welcomed the report as confirming that army and police shot peaceful protesters, and called on President Buhari to ensure that those responsible faced fair trials, along with compensation and guarantees of non-repetition for victims. US Secretary of State Blinken said that if the report named individuals responsible for abuses, there had to be accountability. Activists were cautious. Rinu Oduala said people needed justice and not just reports, and Serah Ibrahim, who gave evidence, said that admitting the events happened was one thing and accountability another.

The UN human rights chief, Michelle Bachelet, said within days of the shooting that she saw little doubt the armed forces had used excessive force, with unlawful killings by live ammunition. In the pages consulted, the army's last recorded position is Brigadier Taiwo's evidence of November 2020 denying that soldiers shot protesters; none of them records the army accepting responsibility. The panel's findings are a state-appointed inquiry's conclusions, not a criminal verdict, and the pages consulted report no prosecution of any soldier, police officer or official.
